title: Peace of mind
hookLine: tranquility comes from letting go of what isn't yours to control

cards: You finally get the quiet weekend. Phone off, a stack of books, a cabin with no signal. Then on Saturday morning a neighbor starts a leaf blower, and keeps it going for an hour.
By noon the real trouble isn't the noise. It's the ruined plan for peace and quiet. There's something funny in that, and Epictetus noticed it long before leaf blowers.
In book four, chapter four, he tells people who want a calm life that they may be chasing it the wrong way.

teach.b: The Greeks had a name for the calm everyone was after: ataraxia. It's built from a verb for stirring up or troubling, the way you'd stir mud in a pond, with a- in front: not. Ataraxia: unstirred.
It wasn't only a Stoic word; Epicureans and Skeptics prized it too, each by its own road. Here's the surprise.
Epictetus says wanting leisure, or quiet, or time to read, can make you just as anxious as wanting money or power. If your peace depends on no leaf blowers, then a leaf blower owns your peace.
Tranquility wanted as an outside condition is one more thing outside your control. He picks on readers in particular. If you can't read and it upsets you, he asks, what was the reading for?
Reading is meant to prepare you for life, not replace it. Someone who reads about calm all day and then snaps at whoever interrupts has missed the point of the book.

teach.h: LET GO OF WHAT ISN'T YOURS.
teach.b: So for Epictetus, peace of mind isn't a place you get to. It's what's left when you stop demanding that things outside you behave. Your judgments, your choices, your effort are yours.
The neighbor's yard tools are not. Let go of the second, and the pond settles by itself, even with the noise still going.
Peace of mind isn't silence. It's not being stirred.

how: Stoics aim for tranquility by distinguishing what is up to them from what isn't, and by practicing calm in ordinary, noisy situations rather than waiting for quiet ones.

a perfectly quiet place, free of all noise

games.why: he says reading is practice for life. if losing your reading time upsets you, the reading hasn't yet done its job.

practice: Don't try to make anything quiet; let the sounds around you keep going, traffic, a fridge, a voice in the next room. Each time one pulls at you, notice it and let it be a sound, outside you, not yours to fix.
The noise is wind across a pond; rest in the still water underneath.

wordCard.voice: Ataraxia. Greek for being unstirred: the calm that comes from letting go of what isn't yours to control, not from finding a perfectly quiet place. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a-, not, and tarassein, to stir up or trouble; calm, unstirred.

carryVoice: Your line: not being stirred. The noise can keep going while the pond settles. That's day four hundred twenty-eight.
